content.intro: This lesson covers Understanding Image Layers. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: An image is a versioned, layered template; a container adds runtime state and a writable layer. Tags are convenient labels that can move, while digests identify content. Prefer trusted, maintained base images and record immutable release identities where reproducibility matters. Learning understanding image layers helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Read-only image layers
items.text: Image layers are shared read-only filesystem changes; each running container has a writable layer whose contents are not a replacement for persistent storage.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
